title: Cross-validation: judging your model reliably
intro: A single train/test split is a gamble. Cross-validation splits your data into k folds, trains k times on all-but-one and averages — plus Stratified/LOO/ShuffleSplit, the choice of k, GridSearchCV and leak-free Pipelines.
keyPoints: A single train/test split is a gamble: the score depends on the random split.
k-fold CV: k alternating splits — the mean is a far more stable estimate.
StratifiedKFold keeps class ratios equal; Leave-One-Out = k = n (expensive).
Combine GridSearchCV + Pipeline: tune hyperparameters without data leakage.

sections.title: The problem with a single train/test split

blocks.html: Which samples land in the test set depends on the random seed: change the seed and your score easily shifts a few percent. One split is one noisy sample.
Feel the noise: the exact same model, ten different seeds — only the split differs. Look at the spread in the output.

blocks.caption: same split, ten different seeds — feel the noise
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import numpy as np

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)

scores = []
for seed in range(10):
    X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(
        X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=seed)
    s = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_tr, y_tr).score(X_te, y_te)
    scores.append(s)
    print(f"seed={seed}:  test-accuracy = {s:.3f}")

print(f"\nmean    : {np.mean(scores):.3f}")
print(f"std     : {np.std(scores):.3f}")
print(f"spread  : {min(scores):.3f} — {max(scores):.3f}")

blocks.html: A single split = one sample from a noisy distribution. If you report a single number, you claim a precision you don't have. Cross-validation fixes exactly this by repeating the split multiple times and averaging.
k-fold CV: split into k folds, repeat k times “train on k−1, score the held-out fold”. Every sample sits in a test fold exactly once; the CV score is the average.

blocks.label: k-fold CV score
blocks.latex: \text{CV-score} \;=\; \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=1}^{k} \text{score}_i, \qquad \text{where}\;\, \text{score}_i = \text{score of the model trained on all folds except fold } i
blocks.caption: The CV score is the mean of the k fold scores — a single number, but based on k different train/test splits.

blocks.html: In scikit-learn nearly a one-liner: cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=k) returns an array of k fold scores. Note: it yields no trained model — only an honest estimate.

blocks.caption: 5-fold CV with cross_val_score
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
import numpy as np

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)

scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5)

print(f"5-fold scores per fold : {np.round(scores, 3)}")
print(f"mean CV score          : {scores.mean():.3f}")
print(f"std across folds       : {scores.std():.3f}")

blocks.html: k = 5 or k = 10 are the standard choices: the std over five folds is typically smaller than over ten single splits.
The cv=k shortcut auto-picks StratifiedKFold (classification) or KFold (regression); for more control pass an explicit splitter. Three variants to know:

rows: splits the data into k contiguous blocks (or shuffled)
regression, or classification with balanced classes
same, but each fold preserves the class ratio
k = n: each fold is exactly one sample (LOOCV)
small datasets (n < 100); slow on large data
takes k random train/test splits; folds may overlap
large data, or when you want fold size independent of k

blocks.caption: KFold vs. StratifiedKFold vs. LeaveOneOut on iris
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import (KFold, StratifiedKFold,
                                     LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score)
import numpy as np

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)

# plain KFold (shuffle on, otherwise iris classes sit in blocks)
kf   = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
skf  = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
loo  = LeaveOneOut()                       # k = n = 150

for name, cv in [('KFold', kf), ('StratifiedKFold', skf), ('LOOCV', loo)]:
    s = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=cv)
    print(f"{name:<18}: {s.mean():.3f}  ± {s.std():.3f}  ({len(s)} folds)")

blocks.html: For classification always StratifiedKFold: without stratification a fold may accidentally contain no positives at all — making its score meaningless.

The choice of k is itself a bias/variance trade-off: larger k = more training data per fold (lower bias), but stronger overlap between train folds (higher variance). LOOCV (k = n) is the extreme case.

blocks.label: MSE of the CV estimate
blocks.caption: The error in your CV estimate compared to the true generalisation score. Bias and variance pull in opposite directions — hence an optimum around k = 5 or 10.

blocks.html: The result is a flattening U-shape: k = 5 and k = 10 sit exactly in the wide flat stretch. Slide the noise sensitivity and watch extreme k values score worse.

blocks.title: Bias–variance of the CV estimate against the number of folds k
blocks.subtitle: More folds = less bias (each fold trains on more data), but slightly more variance (folds overlap more and become correlated). The MSE of the estimate (bias² + variance) drops and then flattens — hence k = 5 or k = 10 as the standard choice.

rows: n fits — slow on large datasets

blocks.html: Rule of thumb: k = 5 for a quick first read, k = 10 if you want a slightly more precise estimate. LOOCV (k = n) you reserve for small datasets (n < 100), where every sample counts.
Tuning hyperparameters on a single test set = secretly overfitting to that test set. The fix: tune with CV on the training data, keep the test set for the final verdict.
GridSearchCV automates it: pass a param_grid and cv=k; scikit-learn cross-validates every candidate, averages and tracks the best — .best_params_, .best_score_, plus one final .score(X_test, y_test).

blocks.caption: Tuning C with 5-fold CV via GridSearchCV
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42)

# pipeline = scaling + logistic regression (see next section)
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))

# tune C via 5-fold CV on the TRAINING set
param_grid = {'logisticregression__C': [0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1, 10, 100, 1000]}
grid = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, cv=5)
grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

print(f"best C         : {grid.best_params_['logisticregression__C']}")
print(f"best CV score  : {grid.best_score_:.3f}")
print(f"score on test  : {grid.score(X_test, y_test):.3f}")

blocks.html: The test set is your final exam: tune with CV on the training data; the model may face the test data once.
Pitfall: fitting a scaler or PCA on the whole dataset before CV leaks test info into the train fold (the scaler “knows” the test fold's mean) — overly optimistic scores.
The remedy: a Pipeline. Pass it to cross_val_score or GridSearchCV, and scikit-learn fits the preprocessing in every fold on the train fold only. No leakage.

blocks.caption: WRONG: fit scaler on all data → leakage
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)

# WRONG: fit scaler on ALL data → test-fold info leaks into train-fold
X_leak = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)
scores_leak = cross_val_score(
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000), X_leak, y, cv=5)

print(f"WITH leakage    : {scores_leak.mean():.3f} ± {scores_leak.std():.3f}")

blocks.caption: RIGHT: Pipeline fits the scaler per fold on the train fold only
blocks.source:
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)

# RIGHT: pipeline fits the scaler fresh in each fold, only on the train-fold
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                     LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000))
scores_clean = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)

print(f"without leakage : {scores_clean.mean():.3f} ± {scores_clean.std():.3f}")

blocks.html: So always use a Pipeline once preprocessing is involved — including GridSearchCV. With aggressive transforms (PCA, feature selection, imputation) leakage can be dramatic.
Parameter names follow the Pipeline syntax: '<step>__<hyperparameter>' — hence 'logisticregression__C'.
The table bundles the choices you make in practice — from the number of folds to whether you need a Pipeline.

rows: k = 5 for speed, k = 10 for slightly more precision, LOOCV when n < 100
Yes → always use a Pipeline, otherwise you leak test info into your train fold
Use GridSearchCV (or RandomizedSearchCV) with CV on the training data — don't touch the test set
When do I report the final score?
Once, on the test set, after tuning. Measuring it multiple times is also a form of leakage

blocks.html: Checklist: test set untouched? Preprocessing in a Pipeline? StratifiedKFold for classification? k sensible (5 or 10)? Both mean and std reported?
